title: Old-Time Cabbage Storage
subtitle: 1917 USDA Wisdom
items: Set heads down in a trench
Dig out a few heads at a time
intro: Old USDA storage bulletins kept late cabbage outdoors in trenches and pits, where it stayed cold and moist without perfuming the house. Here is the old method in our own words.
desc: Old-time cabbage storage inspired by USDA Farmers' Bulletin 879 (1917): pull late cabbage with the roots on, strip loose leaves, set heads down in a well-drained trench and cover with straw and soil so it keeps cold and damp outdoors all winter. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Pressure Can Beef Cubes
subtitle: Shelf-Stable Stew Meat
intro: Canned beef cubes turn into a quick stew or soup on a busy winter night. Meat is low-acid, so it must be pressure canned; these steps follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning.
desc: How to pressure can beef cubes or stew meat the USDA way: trim fat, cut into chunks, brown lightly, pack hot with boiling broth and 1-inch headspace, then process pints 75 minutes and quarts 90 minutes at 10 lb weighted or 11 lb dial gauge pressure (adjust for altitude). Full list on the blog.

title: Keep Chicken Water From Freezing
subtitle: Winter Coop Checklist
items: Keep a thawed spare to swap
Set it out of the wind
Raise it off the cold ground
desc: How to keep backyard chicken water from freezing in winter: use an insulated waterer, check it morning and evening, keep a thawed spare to swap in, set it out of the wind and off the frozen ground, and keep any electric cords well away from dry bedding. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: How to Freeze Carrots
subtitle: Blanch, Chill, Pack
intro: Frozen carrots keep their color and sweetness for months if you blanch them first. Blanching stops the enzymes that make frozen vegetables tough and dull.
desc: How to freeze carrots so they stay sweet and bright: choose young tender carrots, peel and slice them, blanch slices 2 minutes (small whole carrots 5 minutes), cool in ice water, drain and pack in freezer bags or containers. Full list on the blog.

title: Get Ready for a Winter Storm
subtitle: Do This Before It Hits
intro: A winter storm can mean days without power or plowed roads. A few hours of prep before it arrives makes it an inconvenience instead of an emergency.
desc: Winter storm preparedness checklist for homesteaders: store at least 1 gallon of water per person per day, charge phones and power banks, fill the gas tank, refill prescriptions, test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and set out flashlights before the storm hits. Full list on the blog.

title: Plan a Crop Rotation
subtitle: Healthier Beds Next Year
items: Map what grew in each bed
Wait 3 years to repeat a bed
Keep notes in a garden book
intro: Late fall, while you still remember where everything grew, is the best time to plan next year's rotation. Moving crop families around helps cut soil-borne disease and pests.
desc: How to plan a simple vegetable garden crop rotation for beginners: map this year's beds, group crops by plant family, move each family to a new bed every year and wait about 3 years before planting the same family in the same spot. Full list on the blog.
